en: A spear had lodged in his side;
When he seized and wrenched its head,
A blue flame flared.
He had raced upon Kulansur,
And before fair Saikal
Had vied steed against steed.
The great army was caught in the flames,
And spirit-favored Külchoro
Barely escaped death.
Because the mighty Kyrgyz host was there,
Drawing near in a darkened mass, he was saved.
Before this, Sarybai’s
Dread power had become clear,
And the people had despaired of life.
But then Manas appeared,
Dazzling every heart,
Looking vast as blue Song-Köl,
His majesty striking terror into souls,
Making the Kula horse beneath him
Step proudly and high.
He dazzled every heart:
The lion whose patron spirit lived,
The youngest of the six heroes,
A servant of almighty God.
He dazzled every heart,
Appearing before their eyes as though alive.
The wandering saint Khydyr
Came straight forward to lend aid,
Leading the proud-stepping Kula horse,
With twelve noble warriors in his train.
He dazzled every heart,
Appearing like a lofty blue mountain pass.
Such was the man’s form.
He seemed to fill the sky,
Appearing as though alive,
Like an alloy
Of gold and silver,
Like the moon and sun
United in a single being.
Look closely upon this marvel:
He seemed able to pass through the spindle-narrow cleft
Of a gaping gorge.
His vast majesty rose like a glacier;
Not merely Sarybai, but the whole world
He seemed able to conquer if it opposed him.
The horse he rode was Akkula,
Akkula, the racehorse swift as an arrow.
Manas loomed enormous as a hill,
Broad and towering as a blue mountain spur.
The living spirit of your forefather
Stood grandly as his companion,
Taking his place at his right hand.
His destiny was to wreak destruction—
Such was the wonder they beheld.
His forefather, mighty Manas,
Cried, “Stand firm beside my child!”
Shouting in a ringing voice,
He reached out and laid hold,
Supporting him beneath the arm.
He set right what had been broken,
Rejoined what had been severed,
And gathered what had been scattered.
“May the ancestral spirits be my companions,”
Sarybai had once prayed.
But now, “Spirit of my true forefather,
Drive back the bloodthirsty son!
Drive all five claws of the spirit
Into the flank
Of that vaunting boar!”
Then a dazzling vision appeared:
Gray-maned Manas, the leopard,
Seemed like a battle standard
To young warrior Seytek.
“Drive on, my son, drive on!
Seize that slave before you!
Terrify the life from him!
Do not spare him from death—
Steep your spear in blood!”
With Maral at their head, forty men
Shouted before him,
And when he looked, they had become tigers.
A lion opened its jaws,
And the spirit of my heroic father Manas
Grasped Seytek by the hem,
Holding and supporting him without release.
“Do not fear when battle comes!”
Thus brave Seytek
Launched a furious struggle with him.
May God never show us its like!
Clashing their pinewood spears,
Seytek and Sarybai
Stood their ground and thrust at each other.
The earth broke and split,
And all who saw it stood aghast;
Their bosoms filled with clotted blood.
They struck ever harder,
Thrusting face-to-face,
Pressing knee against knee,
Seizing each other’s collars and tugging,
And whenever the gray-maned champions found an opening,
They struck with their fists.
As the fierce conflict mounted,
Those who drew close and saw them
Spared not their lives,
But grappled collar-to-collar.
Their coats were torn to tatters,
Their bodies were gashed all over,
And at every place they struck,
Their clenched hands filled with flesh.
They butted like rams,
Seizing each other’s collars and tugging.
The savage struggle mounted,
They planted their feet and wrestled,
And again the champions came to grips,
Spitting at one another.
Spears, swords, and battle-axes
Were utterly shattered between them.
If you would see a marvel, behold this:
The immense battle thundered,
The wondrous tumult rose,
As Sarybai and brave Seytek
Thrust at one another face-to-face.
Behold the strength of those wrestlers!
Tookyzyl and Kulansur
Were steeds surpassing all other beasts.
In that vast and ruinous battle,
As they met and thrust,
Their coats split and fell in strips,
Their fragile lives were hard-pressed,
And blood streamed and was swallowed.
Their precious, honored heads
Were sorely pressed by spears;
It was a savage battle.
Their eyes dimmed and wandered,
The heroic host that served them
Leaned back, unable to advance,
And began to retreat,
While the two fought without respite.
Their noses were filled with steam,
Their backs and waists ran with sweat,
Their loins bent rigid,
And their dim eyes bulged.
They drove each other onward,
And whenever they collided,
They mauled each other like bull camels.
Such was the nature of the strife.
By day they never rested,
By night they never slept,
Never pausing even when they lay on their sides,
Never lying down long enough to satisfy sleep;
All rest was gone as they fought.
Almighty God alone knew the great cause—
Who had ever seen such a deed?
The people cried out in grief,
And as the two grappled, the black earth
Was torn from its hardened crust.
Seytek and Sarybai
Revealed the full measure of their valor.
Their arrow-proof armor and coats
Were torn apart layer by layer.
So fierce was the mighty battle,
So terrible a sight to behold.
Tookyzyl and Kulansur
Were drenched in crimson blood;
Their entire bodies
Stood motionless and numb,
While every arm and leg
Hung powerless, unable to move.
Such was the contest now.
As the struggle continued,
Tookyzyl turned his head aside.
He was a warrior formidable in cunning,
Sarybai, son of the ogre.
He asked Seytek
For a respite of seven days:
“Since becoming Sarybai,
I have never seen such combat.
I have seen men of immense stature,
And countless mighty men
Who multiplied like seed across the earth.
Against many warriors and many foes
I have fought in combat,
But nowhere on earth, warrior,
Have I seen a youth as valiant as you.
Your heroism is manifest,
Your gray-wolf courage plain;
You are a wolf, brave Seytek!
You are a dread, relentless champion,
A lion, brave Seytek!
The one who grapples and spills blood
Is you, brave Seytek!
To the heroic Kyrgyz people
You are like iron firmly fixed,
A fortress, brave Seytek!
This is while you still bear the name of a boy;
When the flesh fills out upon your calves,
You will drive the whole wide world
Before you and behold it all—
For that were you born, brave Seytek!
In fighting with you,
My courage failed and my strength departed;
The clash of battle has worn me down.
I who never tired am tired,
I who was a lion am exhausted,
I am wearied from fighting.
I began the struggle and have been shaken;
Today I have despaired of life.
Heed the words I speak:
Though you are far greater than I,
Grant me a respite of seven days.
If you truly are a khan,
Stand by your promise!
Swear an oath upon death,
And when the seven days are complete,
When the count reaches the eighth day,
Abide by the words we have spoken.
Then let us fight a mighty battle
And satisfy our hearts’ desire.
Let strength overwhelm the weak;
Let us kill them and thrust them into graves.
Until the seven days have passed,
Until my allotted time is fulfilled,
Let the terms I have spoken take effect.
A good word given in promise
Must hold until its appointed end.
Make your promise firm;
Pledge the mortal oath of men.
Think wisely and do not be rash;
Though the bones of your shins be bent,
Do not flee in childishness,
And do not lose your courage.
If by chance you run away,
It will be a shameful deed.
Mighty son of Manas,
You must keep your promise!”
When brave Seytek heard this,
He agreed to his demand
And granted the ogre’s warrior son
A respite of seven days.
He had all the spears gathered
And brought the whole conflict to a halt.
“Sarybai has taken a seven-day respite,” they said.
To discover whether his word was false or true,
Sarybai withdrew to a secure place
Five stone-throws away.
Before him stood the racehorse Tookyzyl;
Left alone in that desolate place,
He removed its saddle and let it stand bare,
Fettering and hobbling it,
Then tethered it securely
In the roaring icy wind.
Using his white helmet as a pillow,
Keeping his white steel close at hand,
And wrapping himself in his arrow-proof coat,
With his outstretched legs unable to draw back
And his closed eyes unable to open,
